section: Why Not Just Use PubMed Alerts?
text:
Why Not Just Use PubMed Alerts?
PubMed alerts are a reasonable starting point, but they have a key limitation: they give you a flat, unsorted list. If you set up an alert for “inflammatory bowel disease,” every matching paper arrives in the same inbox pile - therapeutics next to epidemiology next to basic science - and you still have to read through everything to find what’s relevant to your work.
IBD LitMonitor takes a different approach. Instead of delivering a raw feed, it organizes papers into sub-fields so you can go straight to the topic area you care about and skip the rest. Each category is collapsible, so browsing the day’s literature takes minutes rather than a lengthy inbox triage.

Search PubMed across category-specific query groups

Publish updated website, RSS feed, and per-category RSS feeds

Why:

Keeps source internals private.
Keeps public history focused on published artifacts.
Makes GitHub Pages hosting straightforward.

title: IBD Literature Report
text:
Papers by Category






NoteHow to Read This Report



Coverage: PubMed queries across a broad set of IBD topic groups, deduplicated - each paper appears exactly once in the most specific matching category.
Categorisation: Automatic and imperfect - a paper found by multiple queries is assigned to the most specific one (e.g. a vedolizumab trial in children goes to Pediatric IBD). For keyword search across all categories or papers from the past 30 days, use the Interactive Dashboard.
Study design badges RCT Meta-analysis Review are shown only when PubMed has explicitly assigned a publication type. Papers published within the last 1-2 weeks often don’t have a badge yet.
★ Flagship journals: Papers from Gut, Gastroenterology, Lancet, NEJM, JCC, and other leading GI journals are marked ★.
Spotted something wrong or have a suggestion?  Send feedback →


Click a category to expand. Click a paper title to read its abstract.


Microbiome & Immunology  (22 papers)



The intestinal microbiome in inflammatory bowel disease and spondyloarthritides.Review  Communications medicine  |  2026-10-24



Extraintestinal manifestations (EIMs) of inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) can affect any organ system, ranging in presentation, frequency, and severity; the most common EIM is IBD-associated arthritis (IAA), an inflammatory arthritis affecting both axial and peripheral joints. IAA is a form of seronegative spondyloarthritis (SpA), which includes multiple arthritides, and those with IAA are also likelier to have other clinical features observed in those with SpA without IBD, such as increased rates of uveitis, psoriasis, and HLA-B27 positivity. These overlapping features are not limited to clinical disease features; the microbiome has been heavily implicated in the development of both IBD and SpA and is associated with non-SpA EIMs. In this review, we offer an overview of several bacterial taxa and associated metabolites that have been identified as differentially abundant in both IBD and SpA, both in stool and mucosal assessment, and how these taxa are associated with differences in intestinal permeability and immune profiles. We also describe how the overlapping dysbiotic microbiome and associated metabolome in IBD, EIMs of IBD, and SpA may differentially modulate the immune system, thus contributing to the shared underlying etiopathogenesis of these diseases. Further work is needed to characterize causal, mechanistic relationships beyond pure computationally identified associations, and apply these findings towards targeted therapeutic intervention and personalized medicine in IBD.


Alizadeh M, Siaton BC, Hudhud D, von Rosenvinge EC, Cross RK, Ravel J


DOI: 10.1038/s43856-026-01919-6  |  View on PubMed →





Bifidobacterium animalis subsp. lactis C-2 Alleviates DSS-induced Ulcerative Colitis via the Microbiota-tryptophan Metabolism-AhR Pathway.  Probiotics and antimicrobial proteins  |  2026-10-24



Inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) is a chronic intestinal disorder closely linked to gut microbiota dysbiosis and metabolic disturbances. This study investigated the alleviating effects and mechanisms of Bifidobacterium animalis subsp. lactis C-2 (C-2) on dextran sulfate sodium (DSS)-induced ulcerative colitis (UC) in mice. The results demonstrated that C-2 significantly ameliorated pathological phenotypes in DSS-induced UC mice, including reduced weight loss, lowered disease activity index (DAI) scores, restored colon length, and diminished inflammatory damage of colonic tissue. Meanwhile, C-2 effectively repaired the intestinal barrier by enhancing the expression of tight junction proteins (Claudin-1, Occludin, ZO-1) and MUC2, thereby reducing lipopolysaccharide in serum and rebalancing pro-inflammatory (TNF-α, IL-6, IL-1β) and anti-inflammatory (IL-10) cytokines in the colon and serum. Notably, C-2 reshaped the gut microbiota structure, significantly increasing microbial diversity (Shannon index) and enriching beneficial bacteria such as Bifidobacterium and Prevotellaceae. Metabolomic analysis further revealed that C-2 modulated the gut tryptophan metabolism pathway, influencing the levels of tryptophan-derived indole metabolites including indole-3-propionic acid (IPA) and indole-3-acrylic acid (I3A), which were associated with activation of the aryl hydrocarbon receptor (AhR)/Cyp1a1 signaling pathway to enhance barrier integrity and suppress inflammation. Moreover, C-2 intervention restored short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs) levels. In summary, C-2 alleviates UC in mice through synergistic mechanisms including optimizing gut microbiota composition, boosting SCFA production, and enhancing tryptophan-derived metabolites. Collectively, these findings support the potential of C-2 as a candidate probiotic intervention strategy for IBD.


Song Z, Wang Z, Ji W, Yu L, Wang X, Xu J, Yuan J, Liang P, Bai X, Wang Y


DOI: 10.1007/s12602-026-11272-8  |  View on PubMed →





Fecal microbiota transplant in the treatment of inflammatory bowel diseases: new perspectives on delivery, mechanism, and clinical positioning.★  Inflammatory bowel diseases  |  2026-10-24



The gut microbiota, a complex and dynamic community of microorganisms, has emerged as a crucial determinant of human health and well-being in recent years. This microbial ecosystem plays a pivotal role in various physiological processes, including nutrient metabolism, immune system regulation, and intestinal homeostasis. Disruptions in the composition and function of the gut microbiota have been implicated in a wide range of diseases, such as Clostridioides difficile infection (CDI) and inflammatory bowel diseases (IBD). The elucidation of the fundamental relationship between human disease and the gut microbiome has positioned fecal microbiota transplantation (FMT) as a transformative strategy in modern clinical practice. However, while FMT is increasingly explored for a diverse range of systemic diseases, its clinical implementation is relatively limited beyond the management of recurrent CDI. This review examines the evolving role of FMT within the therapeutic framework of chronic inflammation, focusing specifically on IBD. We compare the variable clinical outcomes in IBD with the highly successful model of recurrent CDI, highlighting mechanistic and clinical determinants of response in a different disease context. Additionally, we evaluate the progression of delivery strategies, from conventional fecal suspensions to standardized oral capsule formulations, and their implications for efficacy, safety, and scalability. Furthermore, we explore the diversifying clinical scenarios where FMT may be incorporated in the treatment paradigm of IBD, including primary treatment of active inflammation, prevention of relapse, and its place in combination with current immunosuppressive therapies.


Javed A, Chrysostomou D, Marchesi JR, Roberts L, Hart AL, Powell N, Williams HRT, Hicks LC, Mullish BH, Alexander JL


DOI: 10.1093/ibd/izag219  |  View on PubMed →





Clostridium butyricum: A Promising Probiotic for Inflammatory Bowel Disease through Modulation of Gut Microbiota and Immunity.Review  Probiotics and antimicrobial proteins  |  2026-10-24



Inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) is a chronic, relapsing intestinal disorder. Its pathogenesis involves genetic susceptibility, intestinal dysbiosis, environmental triggers, and altered immune responses. Clostridium butyricum (C. butyricum) is a butyrate-producing gut symbiont that has been used as a probiotic for decades. Clinical studies suggest potential benefits in several conditions, including IBD. Here, we review the current evidence on the probiotic mechanisms of C. butyricum in IBD, emphasizing strain-specific effects and distinguishing well-established findings from preliminary ones. The mechanisms discussed include modulation of gut microbiota, improvement of intestinal barrier function, immune regulation, direct antimicrobial activity in preclinical models, and attenuation of oxidative stress. We also highlight unresolved issues, such as strain heterogeneity, limited clinical data, safety concerns in immunocompromised individuals, and the potential role of host genetic factors. Future work should move beyond general probiotic claims and focus on strain-specific, mechanistically defined applications, including genotype-stratified trials to identify patients most likely to benefit.


Zhou Y, Guan Y, Sun P, Zhang J, Shentu D, Rong X, Chen Z


DOI: 10.1007/s12602-026-11268-4  |  View on PubMed →





Baicalin and levofloxacin exert divergent modulation on gut microbiota and metabolome crosstalk in DSS-triggered ulcerative colitis.  Microbiology spectrum  |  2026-10-23



Baicalin (BA), a bioactive flavonoid, and levofloxacin hydrochloride (LH), a fluoroquinolone antibiotic, both hold potential for ulcerative colitis (UC) treatment, yet the mechanistic differences in their regulation of gut microbiota and metabolome remain elusive. This study aimed to systematically compare their therapeutic efficacy and underlying mechanisms in a dextran sulfate sodium-induced murine colitis model, with a focus on gut microbial and metabolic modulation. Mice were randomized into Control, model, BA-treated, and LH-treated groups. Disease severity was assessed via body weight changes, disease activity index, colon length, and histopathological analysis. Western blot and enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay were employed to detect NF-κB pathway activation and pro-inflammatory cytokine levels, while 16S rRNA sequencing and metabolomics profiled gut microbiota and metabolites. Both agents markedly ameliorated colitis symptoms, suppressed NF-κB activation, and cytokine expression, with BA showing superior cytokine inhibition. BA enriched beneficial Lactobacillus, regulating isoflavone/alkaloid synthesis; LH elevated Akkermansia abundance and modulated amino acid metabolism. These findings reveal distinct therapeutic mechanisms of BA and LH, laying a foundation for personalized UC therapy and validating BA’s traditional medicinal utility.IMPORTANCEUlcerative colitis remains a prevalent inflammatory bowel disease with limited microbiota-targeted therapies. Baicalin and levofloxacin both alleviate dextran sulfate sodium-induced colitis, yet their gut microbiome and metabolome regulatory mechanisms have not been directly compared. This study demonstrates that baicalin and levofloxacin exert anti-colitis effects via divergent microbiota-metabolite axes: baicalin enriches Lactobacillus and modulates isoflavone/alkaloid metabolism, while levofloxacin increases Akkermansia and reshapes amino acid metabolism. These distinct mechanisms provide new evidence for developing microbiota-based personalized strategies for ulcerative colitis treatment.


Wang C, Wu W, Cui M, Zhang S, Wang C


DOI: 10.1128/spectrum.01771-26  |  View on PubMed →





Epithelial Barrier-Injury Transcriptomic Stratification Across Human IBD Mucosal Cohorts.  Omics : a journal of integrative biology  |  2026-10-23



Public mucosal transcriptomic datasets provide an opportunity to examine whether experimental epithelial barrier biology is reflected in human inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) endpoints. We constructed a prespecified barrier-injury transcriptomic score from an inositol polyphosphate multikinase-histone deacetylase 3-matrix metalloproteinase (MMP) barrier-biology gene set and epithelial junctional genes, then evaluated it across 10 public IBD mucosal transcriptomic cohorts (2172 scored biopsies) and an independent prospective adult cohort (GSE193677; 1162 participants). Adult cohorts were analyzed for mucosal healing, clinical remission, or treatment response; pediatric and early onset cohorts were analyzed separately. In UNIFI (GSE206285), a higher baseline score was inversely associated with week 8 mucosal healing (odds ratio [OR]: 0.56, 95% confidence interval [CI]: 0.45-0.71, p < 0.001). In GSE193677, the score was associated with IBD compared with control status (OR: 1.71, 95% CI: 1.45-2.02) and with endoscopic and histologic activity. The association was directionally consistent across biopsy-selection analyses and exceeded expression- and variance-matched random-gene estimates (empirical p = 0.034), while MMP and inflammatory comparators were at least as strong. Single-cell data localized the MMP module predominantly to stromal cells. These findings support retrospective transcriptomic stratification of mucosal injury states and define a barrier biology-motivated bulk mucosal readout shaped by stromal inflammatory remodeling in human tissue.


Zheng H, Bu W, Zhuang X


DOI: 10.1177/15578100261499489  |  View on PubMed →





Epidemiological Evidence, Underlying Mechanisms, and Public Health Implications of Ultra-Processed Food Consumption in Inflammatory Bowel Disease.Review  Journal of visualized experiments : JoVE  |  2026-10-23



The overall aim of this narrative review is to synthesize epidemiological evidence linking ultra-processed food (UPF) consumption to the onset and progression of inflammatory bowel disease (IBD), examine the proposed pathophysiological mechanisms, and evaluate contemporary clinical nutritional strategies. Epidemiological data demonstrates a robust, dose-response association between high UPF intake and an increased risk of incident IBD, predominantly Crohn’s disease (CD). Furthermore, in diagnosed patients, UPF consumption correlates with elevated clinical activity, inflammatory relapses, and adverse clinical outcomes. Experimental and observational findings suggest four potential pathways linking UPF-related exposures to altered gut immune homeostasis. First, UPF-rich dietary patterns may be associated with microbiota dysbiosis and reduced short-chain fatty acid (SCFA) availability. Second, experimental studies suggest that selected emulsifiers can alter intestinal mucus organization and epithelial tight-junction integrity. Third, increased intestinal permeability may facilitate exposure to luminal bacterial products and downstream inflammatory signaling through Toll-like receptor 4 (TLR4) and nuclear factor-kappa B (NF-κB). Fourth, advanced glycation end products (AGEs) may contribute to intestinal inflammatory signaling and epithelial stress, although their proposed effects on energy sensing and autophagy in IBD require further validation. Current clinical guidance supports healthy dietary patterns with limited UPF intake and individualized nutritional care, while evidence that UPF restriction alone reduces IBD flares remains insufficient. The review concludes that mitigating the clinical burden of IBD requires integrating personalized nutritional interventions managed by specialized dietitians, while highlighting the necessity for further research into specific food additives and precision nutrition strategies.


Zhang H


DOI: 10.3791/71825  |  View on PubMed →





IL-10-secreting engineered macrophages alleviate DSS-induced colitis with macrophage phenotypic modulation and gut microbiota remodeling in mice.  Bioengineering & translational medicine  |  2026-10-22



Ulcerative colitis (UC) is a chronic recurrent inflammatory bowel disease characterized by abdominal pain, hematochezia, and weight loss. Although remarkable progress has been made toward understanding the pathogenesis of UC, finding more effective treatments for this disease remains a challenge. Interleukin-10 (IL-10) possesses potent anti-inflammatory properties, yet its therapeutic application in UC has failed clinically due to poor targeting and a short half-life. In this study, we developed IL-10-secreting engineered macrophages (IL-10M) based on RAW264.7 cells and evaluated their therapeutic effects in a dextran sulfate sodium-induced colitis model. Intraperitoneal administration of IL-10M alleviated body weight loss, disease activity, colon shortening, and histological injury. IL-10M also reduced mucosal damage and improved tight junction-associated epithelial barrier markers. Flow cytometry further detected engineered macrophage-associated GFP signals in colonic tissues and revealed an early increase in CD206+ endogenous colonic macrophages. Microbiome profiling showed treatment-associated compositional changes, including alterations in Bacteroides acidifaciens and Mucispirillum schaedleri, indicating microbiota remodeling after engineered macrophage treatment. Short-term safety assessment did not reveal overt hematological abnormalities or major histological injury in liver and spleen. Overall, these findings suggest that IL-10-secreting engineered macrophages may represent a promising macrophage-based strategy for mitigating intestinal inflammation in experimental colitis.


Liu H, Liu J, Peng S, Zhao J, Yang F, Zhang L, Wang S, Zhang L, Sun G


DOI: 10.1002/btm2.70178  |  View on PubMed →





Integrating complementary datasets for constructing microbiome-metabolome-disease pathways.  Bioinformatics (Oxford, England)  |  2026-10-20



Microbiome-metabolome-disease pathways play a central role in host health, but studying them is limited by the data available. Large clinical microbiome cohorts often lack metabolomic measurements, while multi-omics studies with paired profiles are typically small or incompletely phenotyped. Combining such complementary datasets is challenging: the metabolite is not measured in the clinical cohort, microbiome data are high-dimensional and compositional, and log-ratio analyses depend on an arbitrarily chosen reference taxon. We propose a framework that integrates a large target cohort that has microbiome and outcome data with a smaller external study that has paired microbiome-metabolome profiles. A high-dimensional structural equation model jointly links the microbiome, the metabolome and the disease outcome. It allows for unmeasured confounding and groups microbes into functional categories. We address compositionality with the additive log-ratio (ALR) transformation, estimate parameters by penalized two-stage least squares, and test metabolite-disease associations with a regularized permutation test. A novel multiple-reference procedure treats each microbe in turn as the ALR reference. It combines the resulting p-values with the Cauchy combination test and classifies microbes by stability selection, which makes inference robust to the choice of reference. In simulations, the method controls the type I error rate, and its power increases with both target and external sample sizes. An application to inflammatory bowel disease, integrating the FRAN and iHMP cohorts, reveals biologically interpretable microbiome-metabolome-disease links. The method is implemented in the R package MMDP, freely available at https://github.com/lei-fang-stat/MMDP. Supplementary data are available at Bioinformatics online.


Fang L, Ye C, Wang Y


DOI: 10.1093/bioinformatics/btag787  |  View on PubMed →





KCTD10 Modulates DSS-induced Ulcerative Colitis via Regulating Intestinal Stem Cell Function.  The American journal of pathology  |  2026-10-20



The incidence of inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) continues to rise annually, which severely threatens public health. While estimates indicate that current therapies cause a 30% IBD clinical treatment failure, the precise pathogenesis remains unclear. Here, we found that a key embryonic development regulator, KCTD10, is correlated with the severity of IBD. We observed enhanced KCTD10 expression during enterocolitis. Intestinal epithelial cell (IEC)-specific knockout of KCTD10 in mice impaired intestinal epithelial barrier function, activated intestinal adaptive immune response, and disrupted intestinal homeostasis. Furthermore, in a dextran sodium sulfate (DSS) -induced ulcerative colitis model, IEC deletion of KCTD10 exacerbated colonic inflammation and impaired post-injury repair. Mechanistically, KCTD10 deletion downregulated intestinal stem cell (ISC) marker genes and affected their function. Importantly, KCTD10 stabilizes the transcription factor ATOH1 by regulating its ubiquitination, thereby determining the fate of intestinal progenitor cells derived from Lgr5+ intestinal stem cells. Our data thus revealed a previously undescribed function of KCTD10 in modulating ulcerative colitis by regulating intestinal stem cell function.


Wang D, Xiao Y, Zhang J, Ding C, Li Z, Ren K


DOI: 10.1016/j.ajpath.2026.10.004  |  View on PubMed →





Crosstalk through cholinergic and aryl hydrocarbon receptor pathways in the anti-inflammatory actions of microbial metabolites.  Naunyn-Schmiedeberg’s archives of pharmacology  |  2026-10-20



The intestinal epithelium maintains immune and metabolic homeostasis at the host-microbiota interface, and its disruption contributes to inflammatory bowel disease (IBD). Microbial metabolites such as short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs) and indole derivatives are known to regulate epithelial and immune functions, but their roles in cholinergic signaling and aryl hydrocarbon receptor (AhR) pathways remain incompletely understood. Caco-2 intestinal epithelial cells were stimulated with lipopolysaccharide (LPS; 10 µg/mL) and co-treated with SCFAs (acetate, propionate, butyrate) or indole derivatives (IAA, IPA, IBA; 1000 µM). The AhR antagonist CH223191 was used to assess receptor involvement. Inflammatory markers (TNF-α, IL-6, COX-2), barrier integrity (FITC-dextran permeability, ZO-1 and occludin), cholinergic components (CHAT, ACHE, BCHE, α7nAChR, mAChR1, mAChR3), and AhR activation (nuclear localization, CYP1A1 expression) were analyzed using qPCR, ELISA, immunostaining, and enzymatic assays. Molecular docking was performed to predict metabolite-protein interactions. LPS induced inflammatory cytokine expression and barrier disruption, whereas SCFAs and indole derivatives significantly reduced inflammation, restored tight-junction organization, and decreased permeability. These metabolites enhanced CHAT and muscarinic receptor expression while suppressing ACHE upregulation, indicating restoration of cholinergic balance. Both groups reactivated AhR signaling, and AhR inhibition disrupted cholinergic regulation, supporting an AhR-dependent mechanism. Butyrate and indole-3-butyric acid exhibited the strongest protective effects. These findings identify a novel AhR-cholinergic axis in intestinal epithelial regulation and highlight microbial metabolites as promising therapeutic candidates for IBD.


Sonmez G, Sari S, Bodur E


DOI: 10.1007/s00210-026-06015-z  |  View on PubMed →





An engineered probiotic for diagnosis and mucosal healing in inflammatory bowel disease.★  Cell reports  |  2026-10-20



Early diagnosis and timely treatment of inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) are critical to limit disease progression, yet integrated diagnostic-therapeutic strategies remain limited. Here, we design a synthetic probiotic system that responds to reactive oxygen species (ROS) to enable noninvasive detection of intestinal inflammation. We further engineer EcN-IL22, a therapeutic strain that conditionally expresses interleukin 22-fragment crystallizable (IL-22-Fc) fusion protein in situ to mitigate colitis-associated tissue damage. Mechanistically, EcN-IL22 activates epithelial IL-22 receptor 1/signal transducer and activator of transcription 3 (IL-22R1/STAT3) signaling, promoting epithelial barrier restoration and intestinal stem cell proliferation. We identify thyroid hormone receptor-interacting protein 13 (Trip13) and fidgetin-like 1 (Fignl1) as IL-22R1-responsive candidate genes associated with epithelial repair. Importantly, replacing the diagnostic output of the ROS-responsive circuit with IL-22-Fc enables inflammation-triggered therapeutic delivery and significantly alleviates colitis. Finally, EcN-IL22 demonstrates robust protective efficacy in a piglet colitis model, supporting its translational potential. Together, this work establishes an integrated probiotic platform for IBD diagnosis and regenerative therapy.


Zhao Y, Sun Y, Zhu X, Hu W, Chen S, Peng G, Yang S, Ma D, Mao X, Yi S


DOI: 10.1016/j.celrep.2026.118171  |  View on PubMed →





Gastrodin alleviates acute colitis with comorbid anxiety- and depression-like behaviours rather than cognitive dysfunction by modulating gut microbiota and suppressing inflammation.  Naunyn-Schmiedeberg’s archives of pharmacology  |  2026-10-19



Inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) patients frequently suffer from emotional disturbances, predominantly anxiety- and depression-like symptoms, and may also have cognitive dysfunction, but the mechanisms remain unclear, and no therapies targeting the gut or nervous system exist. Gastrodin (GAS), the primary active component of Gastrodia elata, has anti-inflammatory and neuroprotective effects. Whether GAS can alleviate acute colitis with comorbid anxiety- and depression-like behaviours or cognitive dysfunction via the gut-brain axis is unknown. Using a 3% dextran sulfate sodium (DSS)-induced mouse model, we administered GAS (240 mg/kg) by gavage for 7 days. The open field, elevated plus maze, tail suspension, and forced swimming tests showed that GAS improved behavioural abnormalities (including anxiety- and depression-like behaviours); it also restored colon length and reduced colonic histopathological injury. Metagenomic sequencing revealed that GAS reshaped the gut microbiota, increasing Sporosarcina and Nitrospirae while decreasing Clostridiaceae and Lachnospiraceae. Untargeted metabolomics indicated that GAS shifted the metabolic profile away from DSS and normalized taurine levels, and KEGG pathway analysis suggested that GAS may partially ameliorate DSS-induced metabolic disturbances by downregulating virulence-related pathways and upregulating energy metabolic pathways such as the TCA cycle and oxidative phosphorylation relative to DSS. Western blot confirmed that GAS restored the tight junction protein Occludin and decreased TNF-α. Quantitative proteomics demonstrated that GAS reversed the aberrant expression of 191 colonic proteins. These results demonstrate correlative associations between GAS treatment and the alleviation of acute colitis and behavioural abnormalities, alongside concurrent changes in gut microbiota composition, metabolite profiles, and intestinal barrier proteins. Whether these associations reflect a causal gut-brain axis mechanism requires direct experimental validation. GAS modulates the microbiota, partially restores metabolism, repairs the gut barrier, and suppresses local inflammation, suggesting a potential gut-brain axis mechanism. These findings position GAS as a promising candidate for further mechanistic and translational investigation in IBD-associated behavioural comorbidities.

However, its clinical presentation is often accompanied by systemic comorbidities that extend far beyond the pelvic cavity, a phenomenon that challenges the traditional disease paradigm. This study aimed to comprehensively assess the associations between endometriosis and autoimmune diseases, allergic conditions, chronic pain syndromes, and endocrine disorders through a systematic review and meta-analysis, thereby providing evidence for redefining endometriosis as a systemic immuno-inflammatory disorder. To conduct this study, a comprehensive search strategy was employed to identify relevant published studies. Electronic databases, including Web of Science and Medline, were searched from their inception up to December 31, 2025. We additionally examined the reference lists of all identified papers to capture any additional articles that were not identified through the electronic database searches. Eligible studies were observational in design (cohort, case-control, and cross-sectional) and reported quantitative data on the association between endometriosis and predefined comorbidities in women. Exclusion criteria included non-human studies, non-English publications, secondary literature types (e.g., reviews, case reports), and studies lacking sufficient data for effect size calculation. Quality assessment was conducted based on the GRADE criteria. The final analysis included 55 studies that met the predefined inclusion criteria and were incorporated into the comprehensive analysis. Of these, 48 studies provided sufficient data for quantitative synthesis (meta-analysis). Specifically, 32 studies investigated the association between endometriosis and autoimmune diseases: 14 on systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE), 8 on Sjögren’s syndrome (SS), 10 on rheumatoid arthritis (RA), 5 on multiple sclerosis (MS), 5 on celiac disease (CLD), and 4 on inflammatory bowel disease (IBD). Additionally, 17 studies examined associations with allergic diseases, 13 focused on pain syndromes, and 6 explored associations with endocrine disorders. Meta-analysis showed that women with endometriosis had a significantly higher risk of certain autoimmune diseases in cohort studies, including SLE (RR: 1.81, 95% CI: 1.50-2.18), SS (RR: 1.54, 95% CI: 1.40-1.71), and RA (RR: 1.71, 95% CI: 1.40-2.09), as well as significantly higher odds in case-control and cross-sectional studies for SLE (OR: 3.93, 95% CI: 2.59-5.98), SS (OR: 3.13, 95% CI: 1.10-8.90), RA (OR: 2.27, 95% CI: 1.75-2.95), MS (OR: 2.30, 95% CI: 1.57-3.37), CLD (OR: 4.50, 95% CI: 1.94-10.42), and IBD (OR: 2.82, 95% CI: 0.58-13.61). Significant associations were also observed for allergic conditions-such as asthma (RR: 1.27, 95% CI: 1.14-1.40) and eczema (OR: 1.58, 95% CI: 1.34-1.87)-and for pain syndromes including fibromyalgia (RR: 1.65, 95% CI: 1.42-1.92), chronic fatigue syndrome (RR: 1.41, 95% CI: 1.31-1.51), and irritable bowel syndrome (RR: 2.51, 95% CI: 1.55-4.07; OR: 3.49, 95% CI: 3.21-3.80). In contrast, no statistically significant increase was observed in the odds of endocrine disorders such as hypothyroidism (OR: 1.89, 95% CI: 0.61-5.90) and hyperthyroidism (OR: 0.95, 95% CI: 0.60-1.52) among women with endometriosis compared with women without endometriosis. However, the overall quality of evidence was generally low or very low according to the GRADE approach, largely due to a high risk of bias in most of the included study designs and statistical analyses. The body of evidence provided by this study supports the reconceptualization of endometriosis as a systemic immuno-inflammatory disease. The associations with various comorbidities are underpinned by shared mechanisms of immune dysregulation and central sensitization. This paradigm shift necessitates a move in clinical practice from a purely gynecological intervention model toward a patient-centered, comprehensive multidisciplinary management approach. It also provides a theoretical foundation for developing novel treatment strategies targeting shared pathological pathways. CRD420251258716.

Maternal and neonatal outcomes in women with inflammatory bowel disease following different biologic utilization trajectories in pregnancy.  European journal of gastroenterology & hepatology  |  2026-10-07



The 2025 Global Consensus recommends continuing biologics throughout pregnancy in women with inflammatory bowel disease. Real-world evidence on biologic treatment patterns and outcomes remains limited. This study compared maternal and neonatal outcomes across different biologic use trajectories during pregnancy. This retrospective study included pregnant women with inflammatory bowel disease treated or delivering at University Hospitals Leuven, Belgium, between 2017 and 2025. Patients were categorized as biologic continuers, discontinuers, non-users, or initiators during pregnancy. Among 211 pregnancies, 75 (35.5%) were continuers, 66 (31.3%) discontinuers, 63 (29.9%) non-users, and seven (3.3%) initiators. Before conception, 66.8% (N = 211) used biologics. Third-trimester disease activity occurred in 42.9% of initiators (3/7), 19.7% of discontinuers (13/66), 18.7% of continuers (14/75), and 17.5% of non-users (11/63). C-sections occurred more in non-users (41.3%, 26/63) and discontinuers (39.4%, 26/66), than in continuers (31.1%, 23/74). Preterm birth was more common among initiators (14.3%, 1/7) and discontinuers (12.1%, 8/66) than continuers (8.0%, 6/75) and non-users (3.2%, 2/62). Low birthweight occurred most in initiators (14.3%, 1/7), continuers (8.1%, 6/74), and discontinuers (6.1%, 4/66). Small-for-gestational-age was numerically more frequent among continuers (14.9%, 11/74) and initiators (14.3%, 1/7), than discontinuers (7.6%, 5/66) and non-users (6.5%, 4/62) (P = 0.21). Discontinuers had numerically more C-sections, preterm births, and third-trimester disease activity than continuers. The numerically higher small-for-gestational-age rate among continuers warrants further investigation. Initiators showed the poorest outcomes, highlighting the need for adequate disease control before and during pregnancy. Larger, confounder-adjusted studies are needed to clarify the relationship between biologic use, disease activity, and outcomes.

IgG N-glycosylation in autoimmune diseases.Review  Frontiers in immunology  |  2026-10-05



IgG is the most abundant antibody in the human circulation. It carries a single conserved glycosylation site, Asparagine 297, in its Fc domain. This N-glycan is critical for the ability of the antibody to activate immune cells via binding to, and cross-linking Fc receptors in order to elicit functional responses. First documented in the context of rheumatoid arthritis (RA), the IgG N-glycan may undergo changes that are correlated to host health. We present a narrative in-depth comparison of changes incurred by IgG N-glycans in autoimmune diseases; RA, systemic lupus erythematosus, multiple sclerosis, type I diabetes, primary biliary cholangitis and inflammatory bowel disease (Crohn’s disease and ulcerative colitis). Based on a systematic literature search, we identify common traits and features that are specific for any one autoimmune disease. Our analysis shows that the single most common trend in most of the conditions analyzed here is increased IgG agalactosylation. Changes to the IgG N-glycan typically accompany and often precede disease onset and flare-ups, while they decrease in remission and pregnancy. The correlation of agalactosylated IgG with inflammatory disease is so striking that the agalactosylated IgG N-glycan has long been viewed as inflammatory and even pathogenic. Yet, despite the association with inflammation, any mechanism by which disease-associated IgG N-glycans may mediate their pro-inflammatory nature remains enigmatic.

Nanoencapsulation of phycocyanin peptides enhances anti-inflammatory activity and alleviates ulcerative colitis.  Journal of the science of food and agriculture  |  2026-10-19



Ulcerative colitis (UC) is a prevalent inflammatory bowel disease, and current medications have considerable side effects. Phycocyanin peptides (PCPs) have demonstrated anti-inflammatory potential; however, their clinical application is limited by poor stability and low bioavailability. This study prepared highly active PCPs via ultrasound-assisted enzymatic hydrolysis and used chitosan-sodium tripolyphosphate nanoencapsulation to improve their application performance. PCPs significantly inhibited nitric oxide release in lipopolysaccharide-induced RAW264.7 cells. The encapsulation efficiency of phycocyanin peptide nanoparticles (PCP-NPs) reached 91.33%, with markedly enhanced gastrointestinal stability and bioavailability. In mouse experiments, PCP-NPs reduced the disease activity index of ulcerative colitis mice, repaired colonic injury, down-regulated pro-inflammatory cytokines, and up-regulated anti-inflammatory cytokines and intestinal tight junction proteins. Three core anti-inflammatory peptides, YAINA, FPYTT, and YVTYA, were isolated and identified. Nanoencapsulation strengthens the anti-inflammatory activity and intestinal barrier repair capacity of PCPs, which hold promising application potential as functional food ingredients for ulcerative colitis prevention. © 2026 Society of Chemical Industry.

Pitfalls in the Diagnosis and Classification of Crohn’s Disease: Misdiagnosis, Overdiagnosis, and Misclassification.Review  The Turkish journal of gastroenterology : the official journal of Turkish Society of Gastroenterology  |  2026-10-06



Crohn’s disease (CD) remains challenging to diagnose and classify accurately despite advances in endoscopy, cross-sectional imaging, intestinal ultrasound, and inflammatory biomarkers. Earlier diagnosis and treat-to-target strategies have improved outcomes but have also increased the risk of misdiagnosis, overdiagnosis, and misclassification of disease activity or severity. Misdiagnosis may expose patients without CD to unnecessary immunosuppressive therapy while delaying recognition and treatment of the true underlying condition, including drug-induced enteropathy, bile acid malabsorption, irritable bowel syndrome, and other disorders of gut-brain interaction. This is particularly relevant in tuberculosis (TB)-endemic regions, where intestinal TB remains one of the most challenging mimics of CD. Overdiagnosis commonly results from overinterpretation of nonspecific symptoms, incidental terminal ileitis, or isolated endoscopic and histological abnormalities. Elevated fecal calprotectin lacks specificity, whereas a low value provides stronger evidence against CD, although it does not reliably exclude isolated small-bowel disease. Misclassification most often reflects underestimation of disease severity, particularly when standard ileocolonoscopy fails to detect proximal small bowel or transmural disease or when discordant endoscopic and cross-sectional imaging findings are not appropriately reconciled. This review examines the major diagnostic and classification pitfalls in CD and proposes a practical, multidisciplinary approach based on integrating complementary investigations, longitudinal reassessment, and diagnostic reconsideration when uncertainty persists.

Safety profile of IL-23 inhibitors from the perspective of physicians and pharmacists: A retrospective real-world pharmacovigilance observational study based on the FAERS database.Observational study  Science progress  |  2026-10-19



ObjectiveInterleukin-23 (IL-23) inhibitors are widely used for psoriasis and inflammatory bowel disease, yet their long-term safety profiles require continual monitoring. This retrospective observational real-world study aimed to detect potential disproportionate reporting signals associated with tildrakizumab, risankizumab, and guselkumab using the FDA Adverse Event Reporting System (FAERS).MethodsAE reports for tildrakizumab, risankizumab, and guselkumab from Q3 2017 to Q3 2025 were retrieved from FAERS. Disproportionality analysis using reporting odds ratios (RORs) was performed, and reported adverse events were classified by system organ classes (SOCs).ResultsA total of 1124, 8574, and 14597 AEs were retrieved for the three IL-23 inhibitors, generating 42, 286, and 348 disproportionate reporting signals, and accumulating 23, 24, and 24 SOCs. Frequently reported AEs included drug ineffectiveness, psoriasis, injection-site reactions, and infections. Disproportionate reporting signals not listed in the current FDA-approved product label comprised cardiovascular events (e.g., myocardial infarction; tildrakizumab ROR = 6.45), malignancies (e.g., malignant melanoma; risankizumab ROR = 8.57), hepatobiliary disorders, and renal complications.ConclusionThese exploratory, hypothesis-generating disproportionate reporting signals may inform routine pharmacovigilance practice for IL-23 inhibitors, alongside well-established common reported events such as infections and systemic reactions. Further pharmacoepidemiologic studies are needed to validate these observations.

Updated treatment targets in inflammatory bowel disease (STRIDE-III): an initiative of the International Organization for the Study of IBD.Review★  The lancet. Gastroenterology & hepatology  |  2026-10-19



Since Selecting Therapeutic Targets in Inflammatory Bowel Disease-II (STRIDE-II), new evidence has become available across inflammatory and patient-centred outcomes. We aimed to update the STRIDE recommendations for Crohn’s disease and ulcerative colitis. We searched MEDLINE, Embase, and Cochrane CENTRAL for studies published after the STRIDE-II search period. Findings were integrated with surveys of International Organization for the Study of IBD (IOIBD) members and paediatric gastroenterologists from the Porto group of the European Society for Paediatric Gastroenterology, Hepatology and Nutrition. Statements were subsequently voted on using a modified Delphi approach; consensus was defined as ≥75% of participants rating a statement 7-10 on a 10-point scale. Of 13 071 records identified in the systematic review, 1018 were included. Surveys were completed by 60 of 79 IOIBD gastroenterologists and 23 of 30 paediatric gastroenterologists in the Porto group. STRIDE-III defines three conceptually distinct categories of treatment targets. Actionable targets include clinical response and remission, which reflect patient priorities, and objective inflammatory targets (C-reactive protein normalisation, faecal calprotectin within target range, and endoscopic remission), supported by interventional evidence demonstrating benefits of target-guided treatment modification. Adjunctive targets (ie, urgency, histological remission in ulcerative colitis, transmural remission in Crohn’s disease, and growth) are supported by studies showing association with favourable outcomes and guide treatment optimisation and tighter monitoring but do not necessarily require a change in therapeutic class. Patient-centred targets (ie, disability, fatigue, and quality of life) directly reflect patients’ well-being and are impaired in a substantial proportion of patients with inflammatory bowel disease; impairment should prompt assessment of inflammation and alternative causes and management through shared decision-making. Targets are further classified as immediate, short-term, intermediate, and long-term. STRIDE-III also defines treatment-specific times to target achievement, new faecal calprotectin thresholds, and adaptations for resource-limited settings. STRIDE-III distinguishes targets that should prompt treatment change from those that primarily guide optimisation and monitoring, while establishing a separate patient-centred pathway based on shared decision-making. This framework supports consistent, evidence-based treat-to-target care.
